unit.can_do_en: say what I do and what I can do.

brief.situation_en: Maria meets Jari at a friend's party.

lines.speaker: Jari
lines.gloss_en: What do you do for work?

judge.reason: Only register differences (sä/sinä, työks/työksesi); same question.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Mä oon asiakaspalvelus. Mut ammatiltani mä oon opettaja.
lines.text_kirja: Minä olen asiakaspalvelussa. Mutta ammatiltani minä olen opettaja.
lines.gloss_en: I work in customer service. But I'm a teacher by profession.

judge.reason: Same content: works in customer service, profession is teacher; only register differences.

puhe.text: Mä oon asiakaspalvelus. Mut ammatiltani mä oon opettaja.

kirja.text: Minä olen asiakaspalvelussa. Mutta ammatiltani minä olen opettaja.

judge.reason: Matikkaa/matematiikkaa and englantii/englantia are colloquial vs standard forms of same words.

lines.speaker: Jari
lines.gloss_en: Great! Do you want to teach in Finland too?

judge.reason: Same exclamation and question; haluuk sä = haluatko sinä.
Joo = kyllä, mun = minun; same meaning.
Kouluis = kouluissa, opettajii = opettajia; same statement.

forms.why_en: The partitive of mikä, what. Mitä saa olla? means What can I get you?
Speech shortens sinä to sä. Books write sinä.
Tehdä changes to tee- and takes -t for 'you': teet.

forms.form_name_en: translative singular, with the possessive ending for your
forms.why_en: Mitä teet työksesi asks 'what do you do for work'. Speech drops -esi: työks.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Speech drops the l and stretches the vowel: olen becomes oon. Books write olen. From olla, to be.
Adds -ssa for 'in': asiakaspalvelu becomes asiakaspalvelussa. Speech shortens -ssa to -s: asiakaspalvelussa becomes asiakaspalvelus.
Speech shortens mutta to mut. Books write mutta.

forms.form_name_en: ablative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Ammatti means profession. -lta with -ni for 'my' gives ammatiltani, 'by profession'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Opettaa means to teach. In the past, with sinä, it becomes opetit.
Teaching a subject takes -a: matematiikkaa. Speech says matikka, giving matikkaa.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive adds -a after puhua, to speak: englantia. Speech turns -ia into -ii.
Exclamations like this take -a: hieno becomes hienoa. Speech turns -oa into -oo.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 2nd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: In Haluuksä, speech says haluu for haluat and -k for -ko, then joins sä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Joo is the everyday spoken yes. Books write kyllä.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Books add -ni for 'my': unelmani. Speech says mun unelma and drops the ending.
Adds -ssa for 'in', with -i- for more than one: kouluissa. Speech says kouluis.
Tarvita means to need. The ending -aan says it is needed without naming who needs it.
Plural 'some' takes -ia: opettaja becomes opettajia. Speech says opettajii.
Toivottavasti means hopefully. It comes from toivoa, to hope.
